nameStory: The name 'lungwort' comes from this lichen's lobed, lung-like appearance that reminded early botaners of human lung tissue. The 'smooth' part distinguishes it from its bumpier cousins - when you run your fingers over its surface, it feels remarkably flat and even, like a piece of smooth leather.
description: Smooth lungwort is a large, leafy lichen that spreads across tree bark in broad, flat lobes. It forms impressive gray patches that can grow quite large over many years, looking almost like someone draped smooth fabric over the tree trunk. When dry, it appears pale gray, but after rain or morning dew, it transforms into a beautiful pale green color. You'll often notice distinctive red-brown spots dotting its surface - these are its reproductive structures called apothecia.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale gray when dry, transforming to soft pale green when wet - like watching the lichen wake up after rain

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Remarkably smooth to the touch, feeling like soft leather or suede without any bumps, ridges, or fuzzy areas

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Large, flat lobes that spread outward from the center, forming broad leafy patches that can cover significant areas of bark

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Abundant red-brown circular spots (apothecia) scattered across the surface, looking like tiny rust-colored buttons

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found growing on tree bark, particularly favoring older trees with rough, stable bark surfaces

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Forms large colonies that can span several inches to over a foot across on mature specimens growing on old trees

habitat: Look for smooth lungwort on the bark of older deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, particularly on oaks, maples, and other hardwoods. It prefers areas with clean air and moderate humidity, so you're more likely to find it in healthier forest environments away from heavy pollution. This lichen thrives in both lowland and montane forests up to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: After spring rains, the lichen shows off its beautiful pale green wet coloration. This is an excellent time to observe the dramatic color change and feel the smooth, slightly swollen texture when moist.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer periods, it appears in its characteristic pale gray state. The red-brown apothecia are often most noticeable against the lighter dry coloration.
seasonality.fall: Frequent fall rains keep the lichen in its green phase more often. The contrast against colorful autumn leaves makes it easier to spot on tree trunks.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round on bare tree trunks, alternating between gray and green states depending on moisture from snow and winter precipitation.

funFact: This lichen can live for hundreds of years and grow incredibly slowly - some of the largest patches you see might have been growing on the same tree since before your great-grandparents were born, expanding outward just millimeters per year!
confusionNotes: It's most often confused with other large foliose lichens on tree bark, but the combination of its perfectly smooth surface and dramatic gray-to-green color change makes it distinctive. Remember: if it feels bumpy, wrinkled, or fuzzy, it's not smooth lungwort!
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name has changed over time - you might see this species listed as either Lobaria quercizans or Ricasolia quercizans in different field guides, but both names refer to the same smooth lungwort lichen.
compareHints: Since smooth lungwort is the only Ricasolia species commonly found in New England, compare it with other large leafy lichens in the related Lobariaceae family. Unlike the more common tree lungwort (Lobaria pulmonaria), smooth lungwort lacks the network of ridges and valleys that give other lungworts their textured, lung-like surface. The perfectly smooth texture combined with the gray-to-green color change is your best identifying feature.
